planting.note: Wedge the tuberous base into a shaded, vertical or steeply sloped rock crevice with about a third of the tuber left exposed; unheated alpine frames also suit it.

directions: Native to shaded rock faces and conglomerate cliffs from the Himalaya into western China, this acaulescent gesneriad forms a tight rosette of hairy, fan-shaped leaves atop a woody, caudex-like tuber. Clusters of small two-lipped blue-to-violet flowers appear on short stalks from the rosette center. It thrives wedged into vertical crevices or scree with its roots in deep, humus-rich leaf litter and the crown kept dry and shaded. Grown mainly by alpine and rock-garden specialists through seed exchanges and crevice-garden nurseries.
sources: Alpine Garden Society seed and plant lists

planting.note: Set rhizomatous divisions in humus-rich, well-drained shaded soil; good winter drainage is essential since the plant has proven hardy well below freezing when kept dry at the crown.

directions: The sole species in its genus, Titanotrichum oldhamii is a surprisingly cold-hardy African-violet relative from Taiwan, Fujian, and the Ryukyu Islands that forms a basal clump of fuzzy, toothed leaves. In early autumn it sends up spikes of showy, golden-yellow tubular flowers marked with cinnamon-red throats, resembling a cross between a foxglove and a gesneriad. It also reproduces by small plantlets formed on spent flower spikes, making it easy to share. Best in open, humus-rich shaded woodland soil with sharp winter drainage; carried by several specialty perennial nurseries in the US and UK.

planting.note: Grow in a free-draining, acid-to-neutral mix mimicking mossy bark or rock, in sheltered bright shade; container culture with winter protection is safest outside mild climates.

directions: A suckering, evergreen shrublet from East Asian forests that naturally clings to shaded, mossy rock faces and tree bark, Lysionotus pauciflorus bears small glossy, toothed leaves and pendant, pale purple tubular flowers striped inside the throat. It prefers bright, even shade and consistent moisture with excellent drainage, much like an epiphytic gesneriad grown on a slab. Hardier mountain forms collected at higher elevation extend its usable range beyond the typical zone 9 limit. Available mainly from plant-collector nurseries that specialize in Asian woodland and epiphytic species.

planting.note: Start seed indoors with a cold period before germination, then plant out after frost into humus-rich soil at a woodland edge where the brittle twining stems can scramble through shrubs.

directions: A slender twining perennial from forest clearings in Sichuan and Yunnan, this Codonopsis produces open, saucer-shaped violet-blue flowers rather than the typical bell shape of its relatives. The brittle stems need the support of surrounding shrubs or a twig support and benefit from shelter from wind. It dies back to a tuberous rootstock each winter and resents root disturbance once established. Grown from seed sourced through specialty seed houses, it rewards patient gardeners with an unusual late-summer woodland-edge display.

planting.note: Give seedlings a cold spell before germination and transplant into woodland soil with shrubby support for the scrambling stems; plants resent disturbance once sited.

directions: This Central Asian relative of Campanula scrambles through nearby shrubs and bears nodding, pale ice-blue bells painted inside with maroon, black, and orange veining around the throat, visible when the flower is tipped up to view. The crushed foliage and tuberous roots carry the mild foetid-alliaceous scent typical of the genus, giving it the alternate name poor man's ginseng. It is one of the more reliably hardy Codonopsis species and tolerates a woodland or partly shaded border position better than its tender relatives. Listed by several UK and European seed specialists and carried by RHS-affiliated trial gardens.

planting.note: Plant tubers in autumn in shaded, humus-rich, free-draining soil; foliage and hooded flowers appear through winter with summer dormancy, so mulch lightly and avoid summer irrigation.

directions: A close relative of the mouse plant, Friar's cowl forms low clumps of long-stalked, arrow-shaped leaves topped by small flowers wrapped in a curved, hooded spathe reminiscent of a monk's cowl, dark brown-purple with a pale stripe. It is winter-active and summer-dormant, emerging with the first autumn rains and flowering from late autumn into spring before dying back to the rhizome for a dry summer rest. Best naturalized under deciduous shrubs or trees in woodland soil that dries somewhat in summer, matching its Mediterranean scrub and olive-grove origins. Offered by specialty bulb nurseries alongside its relative Arisarum proboscideum.

planting.note: Set divisions into humus-rich, evenly moist woodland soil in dappled or deep shade after frost danger passes; higher-elevation collected forms tolerate more cold than typical lowland stock, but treat as tender/subtropical and protect or pot up in all but the mildest zones.

directions: A variable species from Taiwan and southern China through the Himalayan foothills, this begonia bears asymmetrical, deeply lobed palmate leaves often marked with bronze or purple along the veins, and small pink to white flowers in loose cymes over summer. It wants cool morning light only, rich moist humus, and protection from hot afternoon sun, and is best treated as a tender to half-hardy container or greenhouse subject outside the warmest zones. Distributed through hardy-begonia and tropical-foliage specialist nurseries rather than general garden centers.

planting.note: Repot pseudobulbs each January into a free-draining bark-and-perlite mix in a shaded, frost-sheltered spot such as a cold frame or shaded woodland pot bed; keep dry and cold through winter dormancy.

directions: A Yunnan native among the hardiest of the terrestrial Pleione orchids, producing solitary golden-yellow to apricot flowers with a fringed, spotted lip in early spring before the single pleated leaf fully expands. Pseudobulbs need a dry, cold winter rest followed by regular water and feeding through the growing season, with 50 to 70 percent shade and no direct sun. It is best grown in shallow pots or pans that can be moved under cover in hard winters, or bedded in a sheltered shaded trough in milder gardens. Supplied by specialist hardy-orchid nurseries in the UK and by orchid societies' bulb exchanges.
